column2: From Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whatever I have forbidden you, avoid it; and whatever I have commanded you, do of it as much as you are able. For what destroyed those before you was only their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets.”
Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Muslim alone recorded this hadith in this wording, in the narration of al-Zuhrī from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Abū Salamah, both from Abū Hurayrah. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it in the narration of Abū al-Zinād, from al-Aʿraj, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ,

who said: “Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone. What destroyed those before you was only their questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets. So when I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you something, do of it as much as you are able.” Muslim recorded it by two other routes from Abū Hurayrah with the same meaning.
One of Muslim's narrations mentions the occasion of this hadith, in the narration of Muḥammad ibn Ziyād from Abū Hurayrah, who said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us and said: “O people, Allah has made Ḥajj obligatory on you, so perform Ḥajj.” A man said: Every year, O Messenger of Allah?
He remained silent until the man had said it three times. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it.” Then he said: “Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone, for those before you were destroyed only by their questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets. When I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able; and when I forbid you something, leave it.”

Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it by another route in abridged form, and in it he said: Then His words, the Exalted, were revealed: “O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you” [al-Māʾidah 5:101].
It has been narrated by more than one route that this verse was revealed when they asked the Prophet ﷺ about Ḥajj, saying: Is it every year?
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Anas said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us, and a man said:
Who is my father? He said: “So-and-so.” Then this verse was revealed: “Do not ask about things.”
Also in both, from Qatādah, from Anas, who said: People questioned the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until they pressed him hard with their questions, and he became angry. He mounted the pulpit and said:

“You will not ask me about anything today but I will explain it to you.” A man stood up who, whenever he quarrelled with people, was called the son of someone other than his father. He said: O Messenger of Allah, who is my father?
He said: “Your father is Ḥudhāfah.” Then ʿUmar spoke up and said: We are pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion and with Muḥammad as Messenger; we seek refuge with Allah from trials.
When narrating this hadith, Qatādah used to mention this verse: “O you who believe, do not ask about things.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿAbbās said: Some people used to question the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in mockery. A man would say: Who is my father?
And a man whose she-camel had strayed would say: Where is my she-camel?
So Allah revealed this verse: “O you who believe, do not ask about things.”
Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded in his Tafsīr from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, who said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out angry, his face reddened, and sat on the pulpit. A man stood up before him and said: Where am I [to end up]?
He said: “In the Fire.” Another stood up before him and said: Who is my father?

He said: “Your father is Ḥudhāfah.” ʿUmar stood up and said: We are pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, with Muḥammad as Prophet and with the Qurʾān as guide. O Messenger of Allah, we have only lately come out of the Jāhiliyyah and shirk,
and Allah knows best who our fathers are. His anger then subsided, and this verse was revealed: “O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you.”
He also narrated by way of al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words, “O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you,” that he said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made a proclamation among the people, saying: “O people, Ḥajj has been prescribed for you.” A man stood up and said: O Messenger of Allah, every year?

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was made extremely angry, and said: “By Him in whose hand is my soul, if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory; and if it had become obligatory you would not have been able to do it,

and then you would have disbelieved. So leave me alone as long as I leave you alone. When I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able; and when I forbid you something, refrain from it.” And Allah revealed:

“O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you.” He forbade them to ask for the like of what the Christians asked for in the matter of the Table, after which they became disbelievers in it.

So Allah the Exalted forbade that, and said: Do not ask about things which, if the Qurʾān were revealed about them with severity, would distress you. Wait instead, for when the Qurʾān is revealed, you will not ask about anything without finding its explanation.
These hadiths, then, show that it is forbidden to ask about needless things whose answer would distress the questioner — such as a questioner asking whether he is in the Fire or in Paradise,

or whether his father is the man he is attributed to or someone else — and that it is forbidden to ask in order to make difficulties, or in idle play or mockery, as many of the hypocrites and others used to do.

Close to this is asking for signs and demanding them in order to make difficulties, as the polytheists and the People of the Book used to ask of him; ʿIkrimah and others said that the verse was revealed about that.
Close to it, too, is asking about what Allah has hidden from His servants and not disclosed to them, such as asking about the time of the Hour, and about the spirit.

They also show that the Muslims were forbidden to ask about many matters of the lawful and the unlawful where it was feared that the question might cause something stricter to be revealed, such as asking whether Ḥajj is obligatory every year or not.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Saʿd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Muslim who commits the greatest crime against the Muslims is one who asks about something that had not been made unlawful, and it is made unlawful because of his question.”

When the Prophet ﷺ was asked about liʿān, he disliked such questions and found fault with them, until the man who had asked about it before it happened was himself afflicted with it in his own family. The Prophet ﷺ used to forbid idle gossip, excessive questioning and wasting wealth.

The Prophet ﷺ allowed only the Bedouins and similar delegations who came to him to ask questions, to win their hearts. As for the Emigrants and the Helpers living in Madīnah, in whose hearts faith was firmly rooted, they were forbidden to ask,

as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, who said: I stayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madīnah for a year, and nothing kept me from emigrating but the asking of questions: when one of us emigrated, he would no longer ask the Prophet ﷺ.

Also in it, from Anas, who said: We were forbidden to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about anything, so we used to be delighted when an intelligent man from the desert came and asked him while we listened.
In the Musnad, Abū Umāmah said: Allah had revealed: “O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you.” So we had come to dislike asking him much,
and we guarded against it once Allah had revealed that to His Prophet ﷺ. So we went to a Bedouin, bribed him with a cloak, and said to him: Ask the Prophet ﷺ — and he mentioned a hadith.

In the Musnad of Abū Yaʿlā, al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib said: A whole year would pass in which I wanted to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about something but held back out of awe of him; and we used to long for the Bedouins to come.
In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, Ibn ʿAbbās said: I have never seen a people better than the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ. They asked him only twelve questions,

all of them in the Qurʾān: “They ask you about wine and gambling” [al-Baqarah 2:219], “They ask you about the sacred month” [al-Baqarah 2:217], “And they ask you about orphans” [al-Baqarah 2:220] — and he mentioned the rest of the hadith.

The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ did sometimes ask him for the ruling on events before they happened, but in order to act on it when they did happen — as when they said to him: We are going to meet the enemy tomorrow and we have no knives with us; may we slaughter with reeds?
They asked him about the rulers he told them would come after him, about obeying them and fighting them; and Ḥudhayfah asked him about the trials, and what he should do in them.

This hadith, then — his words ﷺ, “Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone, for those before you were destroyed only by their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets” — shows that questions are disliked and blameworthy.

Some people, however, claim that this applied only to the time of the Prophet ﷺ, because of what was feared then: that something not yet forbidden might be forbidden, or something hard to carry out made obligatory. After his death ﷺ there was no longer any danger of that.

But this is not the only reason questions are disliked. There is another, the one Ibn ʿAbbās pointed to in the words of his we quoted: Wait instead, for when the Qurʾān is revealed, you will not ask about anything without finding its explanation.
This means that everything the Muslims need in their religion Allah will certainly make clear in His Mighty Book, and His Messenger will convey it from Him; after this, no one has any need to ask.

For Allah the Exalted knows His servants' interests better than they do, and whatever brings them guidance and benefit Allah will certainly make clear to them from the outset, without their asking, as He said:

“Allah makes this clear to you lest you go astray” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]. There is then no need to ask about anything, especially before it happens and is needed. The pressing need is rather to understand what Allah and His Messenger have told us,

and then to follow it and act on it. The Prophet ﷺ used to be asked questions and would refer the questioner to the Qurʾān, as when ʿUmar asked him about kalālah [one who dies leaving neither parent nor child], and he said: “The summer verse is enough for you.”
In this hadith he ﷺ indicated that being occupied with obeying his commands and avoiding his prohibitions leaves no room for questions, saying: “When I forbid you something, avoid it,
and when I command you something, do of it as much as you are able.” What the Muslim must concern himself with and attend to is searching out what has come from Allah and His Messenger ﷺ,
then striving to understand it and grasp its meanings, and then occupying himself with affirming it if it concerns matters of belief; and if it concerns matters of practice,
doing his utmost to carry out whatever commands he is able to and to avoid what is forbidden, with his attention wholly turned to that
and to nothing else.
Such was the way of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and of those who followed them in excellence in seeking beneficial knowledge from the Book and the Sunnah.

If, however, the listener's attention, on hearing a command or a prohibition, turns to supposing things that may or may not happen, this falls under the prohibition and saps his earnestness in following the command.
A man asked Ibn ʿUmar about touching the Black Stone, and he said to him: I saw the Prophet ﷺ touching it and kissing it. The man said to him: What if I am prevented from reaching it?
What if I am crowded out?
Ibn ʿUmar said to him: Leave your “what if” in Yemen! I saw the Prophet ﷺ touching it and kissing it. Al-Tirmidhī recorded it.
What Ibn ʿUmar meant was: Let your only concern be to follow the example of the Prophet ﷺ; there is no need to suppose, before it happens, that you will be unable to do so or will find it difficult,

for that may weaken one's resolve to follow him. Seeking understanding of the religion and asking about knowledge are praiseworthy only when they are for the sake of action, not for wrangling and dispute.
It is narrated that ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned trials that would come at the end of time, and ʿUmar said to him: When will that be, ʿAlī?
He said: When understanding is sought for other than the religion, knowledge is learned for other than practice, and this world is sought through the deeds of the Hereafter.

Ibn Masʿūd said: How will you be when a trial envelops you in which the young grow up and the old grow decrepit, and which is taken as a Sunnah, so that if it is changed one day people say: This is objectionable?
They said: When will that be?

He said: When your trustworthy ones are few and your rulers many, your jurists few and your reciters many, when understanding is sought for other than the religion, and this world is sought through the deeds of the Hereafter.
ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded both of them in his book.
For this reason many of the Companions and Successors disliked being asked about events before they happened, and would not answer such questions. ʿAmr ibn Murrah said:
ʿUmar came out to the people and said: I forbid you, on pain of sin, to ask us about what has not happened, for what has happened keeps us busy enough.
Ibn ʿUmar said: Do not ask about what has not happened, for I heard ʿUmar curse anyone who asked about what had not happened.
When Zayd ibn Thābit was asked about something, he would say: Has this happened?
If they said no, he would say: Leave it until it happens.
Masrūq said: I asked Ubayy ibn Kaʿb about something, and he said: Has it happened yet?
I said: No. He said: Then spare us — meaning, give us rest — until it happens; when it does, we will exert our judgement for you.
Al-Shaʿbī said: ʿAmmār was asked a question, and he said: Has this happened yet?
They said: No. He said: Then leave us until it happens; when it does, we will take the trouble over it for you.
Al-Ṣalt ibn Rāshid said: I asked Ṭāwūs about something, and he rebuked me and said: Has this happened?
I said: Yes. He said: By Allah?
I said: By Allah. He said: Our companions told us that Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: O people, do not hasten the trial before it comes down, or you will be led off this way and that;
for if you do not hasten the trial before it comes down, the Muslims will never be without someone among them who, when asked, is set right, or, when he speaks, is guided to what is correct.
Abū Dāwūd recorded it in Kitāb al-Marāsīl as marfūʿ (the Prophet's words), by way of Ibn ʿAjlān, from Ṭāwūs, from Muʿādh, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Do not hasten the trial before it comes down, for if you do not, the Muslims will never be without someone among them who, when he speaks, is set right or guided to what is correct; but if you hasten it, the paths will scatter you this way and that.”
Its being mursal means that Ṭāwūs did not hear from Muʿādh.
He also recorded it in the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from Abū Salamah, from the Prophet ﷺ, with the same meaning, as a mursal report.
Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Minhāl narrated: Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim told us: I heard al-Zubayr ibn Saʿīd relate that a man of Banū Hāshim said: I heard our elders relate that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“There will always be among my Ummah someone who, when asked, is set right and guides aright, until they ask about things whose explanation has not been revealed; when they do that, they will be led off this way and that.”
Al-Ṣunābiḥī narrated from Muʿāwiyah, from the Prophet ﷺ, “that he forbade aghlūṭāt [trick questions].” Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) recorded it.
Al-Awzāʿī explained it, saying: They are hard, knotty questions.
ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus said: They are needless questions of the “how this and how that” sort.
It is narrated from the hadith of Thawbān that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There will be people of my Ummah who try to trip up their jurists with difficult questions; they are the worst of my Ummah.”
Al-Ḥasan said: The worst of Allah's servants are those who chase after the worst of questions to bewilder Allah's servants with them.
Al-Awzāʿī said: When Allah wishes to deprive His servant of the blessing of knowledge, He casts trick questions onto his tongue; and I have seen such people to be the least knowledgeable of all.
Ibn Wahb reported that Mālik said: I knew this city when its people disliked the profusion that people indulge in today — meaning questions.
He also said: I heard Mālik finding fault with much talk and many fatwas. Then he said: He speaks like a camel in rut, saying, It is such-and-such, it is such-and-such — braying away as he talks.

He said: I heard Mālik disliking answering a great many questions, and he said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And they ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the affair of my Lord” [al-Isrāʾ 17:85] — and no answer came to him on the matter.
Mālik also disliked arguing in defence of the Sunnah.
Al-Haytham ibn Jamīl said: I said to Mālik: O Abū ʿAbdillāh, may a man who knows the Sunnah argue in its defence?
He said: No; but he should state what the Sunnah is. If it is accepted from him, well and good; otherwise he should keep silent.
Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā said: Mālik used to say: Wrangling and arguing about knowledge take away the light of knowledge from a man's heart.
Ibn Wahb said: I heard Mālik say: Wrangling about knowledge hardens hearts and breeds rancour.

Abū Shurayḥ al-Iskandarānī was in his circle one day when the questions multiplied, and he said: Your hearts have grown grimy since this morning. Go to Abū Ḥumayd Khālid ibn Ḥumayd and polish your hearts,

and learn these exhortations (raghāʾib), for they renew worship, give rise to detachment from the world and draw friendship. Ask few questions, except about what has actually happened, for questions harden hearts and breed enmity.
Al-Maymūnī said: I heard Abū ʿAbdillāh — meaning Aḥmad — being asked a question, and he said: Has this question actually arisen?
Have you been faced with it yet?
People have divided into several groups on this matter.

Some followers of the hadith scholars closed the door of questions so completely that their understanding and knowledge of the limits of what Allah revealed to His Messenger dwindled, and they became carriers of jurisprudence who were not themselves jurists.

Some jurists among the people of opinion (ahl al-raʾy) went to great lengths in generating questions before they happened — those that usually happen and those that do not — and busied themselves with laboured answers to them and with much quarrelling and arguing over them, until hearts became divided as a result,

and whims, malice, enmity and hatred settled in them because of it. This is often coupled with the intention of besting others, seeking superiority and boasting, and turning people's faces towards oneself. This is what the godly scholars condemned, and the Sunnah shows it to be ugly and unlawful.

As for the jurists among the hadith scholars who act on the hadith, their chief concern is to search out the meanings of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the authentic Sunnah that explains it, and the words of the Companions and of those who followed them in excellence;

and to search out the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, knowing what is sound in it and what is unsound, then gaining understanding of it, comprehending it and grasping its meanings; and then knowing the words of the Companions and of those who followed them in excellence in the various branches of knowledge — Qurʾān commentary and hadith,
questions of the lawful and the unlawful, the foundations of the Sunnah, zuhd, heart-softening counsels and so on. This is the way of Imam Aḥmad and of the godly hadith scholars who agreed with him.

Knowing all this is occupation enough to keep one from busying oneself with newly devised opinion that brings no benefit and never happens in practice, and arguing over which only breeds quarrels, disputes and endless gossip.
Imam Aḥmad, when asked about one of these contrived questions that do not happen, would often say: Spare us these newfangled questions.

How well Yūnus ibn Sulaymān al-Saqaṭī put it: I looked into the matter and found it to be either hadith or opinion. In hadith I found mention of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, His lordship, His majesty and His greatness;

mention of the Throne and the description of Paradise and the Fire; mention of the prophets and messengers, the lawful and the unlawful, and encouragement to keep ties of kinship — all good gathered together in it. Then I looked into opinion and found in it cunning, treachery, legal stratagems and the severing of kinship — all evil gathered together in it.
Aḥmad ibn Shabbawayh said: Whoever wants the knowledge of the grave should keep to the reports; whoever wants the knowledge of bread should keep to opinion.
Whoever follows the way of seeking knowledge that we have described will usually be able to understand the answer to events that actually occur,

because their roots are found in the foundations we have referred to. This path must be followed behind the imams of the religion whose right guidance and understanding are agreed upon, such as al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and those who followed their way;
for whoever claims to follow this path in some way other than theirs falls into trackless deserts and places of ruin, adopts what may not be adopted and abandons what must be acted on.

The crux of the whole matter is that one should seek by it the Face of Allah and nearness to Him, through knowing what He revealed to His Messenger, following his way, acting on it and calling people to it.

Whoever is like that, Allah will grant him success and keep him on the right course, inspire him with right guidance and teach him what he did not know, and he will be among the scholars praised in the Book, in His words, the Exalted:
“Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah” [Fāṭir 35:28], and among those firmly grounded in knowledge. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded in his Tafsīr, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ,

that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about those firmly grounded in knowledge, and he said: “One whose oath is kept, whose tongue is truthful and whose heart is upright, and whose stomach and private parts are chaste — that is one of those firmly grounded in knowledge.”

Nāfiʿ ibn Yazīd said: It is said that those firmly grounded in knowledge are those humble before Allah, abasing themselves before Allah in seeking His pleasure, who do not reach for what is above them nor look down on those below them.
This is supported by the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “The people of Yemen have come to you; they are the kindest of heart and the most tender of soul.
Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni and wisdom is Yemeni.”

Here he was pointing to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and the scholars of the people of Yemen who followed his way, and after them to the likes of Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī, Uways al-Qaranī, Ṭāwūs, Wahb ibn Munabbih and other scholars of the people of Yemen.

All of these were godly scholars who feared Allah; all of them knew Allah, stood in awe of Him and feared Him. Some had wider knowledge than others of Allah's rulings and the laws of His religion, but what set them apart from other people was not endless talk, nor research, nor argument.

Likewise Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), the most knowledgeable of people about the lawful and the unlawful, who will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection a stone's throw ahead of the scholars.

His knowledge did not lie in multiplying and expanding questions; on the contrary, we have seen that he disliked talking about what had not happened. He was a knower of Allah and a knower of the foundations of His religion.
Imam Aḥmad was asked: Whom shall we ask after you?
He said: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq. He was told: He does not have broad knowledge. He said: He is a righteous man, and someone like him is granted success in hitting upon the truth.
He was asked about Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, and said: He had the root of knowledge: fear of Allah.
This goes back to the saying of one of the Salaf: Fear of Allah is knowledge enough, and being deluded about Allah is ignorance enough.
This is a vast subject, which would take long to cover fully.

Let us return to the commentary on the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him). We say: whoever does not busy himself with multiplying questions the like of which are not found in the Book or the Sunnah,

but busies himself with understanding the words of Allah and His Messenger, aiming thereby to obey the commands and avoid the prohibitions, is one who has obeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this hadith

and acted on what it requires. But whoever does not concern himself with understanding what Allah revealed to His Messenger, and busies himself with generating questions that may or may not happen and labouring over their answers by mere opinion, is in danger of contravening this hadith, committing what it forbids and abandoning what it commands.

Know that the frequent occurrence of events that have no basis in the Book and the Sunnah comes only from neglecting to obey the commands of Allah and His Messenger and to avoid the prohibitions of Allah and His Messenger.

If whoever wanted to do something asked what Allah has prescribed for that deed and complied with it, and asked what He has forbidden and avoided it, events would happen within the bounds of the Book and the Sunnah.

It is only because people act according to their own opinions and desires that events mostly happen in contradiction to what Allah has prescribed, and it may be hard to trace them back to the rulings found in the Book and the Sunnah, because they are so far removed from them.

In short, whoever obeys what the Prophet ﷺ commanded in this hadith, refrains from what he forbade, and is occupied with that rather than anything else, will attain salvation in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever goes against it and busies himself with his own notions and with what he deems good falls into what the Prophet ﷺ warned against: the state of the People of the Book, who were destroyed by their excessive questioning, their disagreeing with their prophets and their failure to submit to and obey their messengers.

His words ﷺ, “When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you something, do of it as much as you are able”: some scholars said that one can infer from this that prohibition is stricter than command,
because no allowance was given for committing any part of what is prohibited, while the command was limited according to ability. This is narrated from Imam Aḥmad.
Similar to this is the saying of one of them: Deeds of righteousness are done by the righteous and the wicked alike, but sins are left only by the truthful (ṣiddīq).
It is narrated from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “Guard against forbidden things and you will be the most devout of people.”
ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: Whoever would like to outstrip the tireless striver should refrain from sins. It is also narrated from her as marfūʿ.
Al-Ḥasan said: The worshippers have not worshipped with anything better than leaving what Allah has forbidden them.

It appears that what has come about preferring the leaving of forbidden things over doing acts of obedience refers only to voluntary acts of obedience; otherwise obligatory deeds as a category are better than leaving forbidden things as a category,

because deeds are sought for their own sake, while with forbidden things what is sought is their absence; that is why leaving them needs no intention, unlike deeds. Likewise, leaving deeds as a category may amount to disbelief, as with abandoning tawḥīd, or abandoning the pillars of Islam or some of them, as discussed earlier,

whereas committing forbidden things does not in itself entail disbelief. This is supported by Ibn ʿUmar's saying: Returning a single dāniq of unlawful money is better than a hundred thousand spent in the way of Allah.
One of the Salaf said: Leaving a single dāniq of what Allah dislikes is dearer to me than five hundred pilgrimages.
Maymūn ibn Mihrān said: Remembering Allah with the tongue is good, but better than that is for the servant to remember Allah when about to sin, and hold back from it.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: To return a single dirham of doubtful origin is dearer to me than giving a hundred thousand in charity, and another hundred thousand — until he reached six hundred thousand.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: Taqwā is not standing in prayer by night and fasting by day while mixing good and bad in between; taqwā is performing what Allah has made obligatory and leaving what Allah has made unlawful. If there are deeds besides that, it is good upon good — or words to that effect.
He also said: I wish I prayed nothing but the five prayers, apart from witr, paid zakāh and never gave a dirham in charity after it, fasted Ramaḍān and never fasted another day after it,
and performed the Ḥajj of Islam and never performed Ḥajj again — and then took my surplus strength and devoted it to what Allah has made unlawful for me, holding back from it.
The upshot of their words is that avoiding forbidden things, however small, is better than doing many voluntary acts of obedience, since the former is obligatory and the latter supererogatory.
A group of later scholars said: He ﷺ said, “When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you something, do of it as much as you are able,”

only because obeying a command requires action, and action depends for its existence on conditions and means, some of which may be beyond one's ability; so he limited it by ability, just as Allah limited the command to taqwā by ability, saying, the Exalted: “So be mindful of Allah as much as you are able” [al-Taghābun 64:16].
And He said of Ḥajj: “And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people — whoever is able to find a way to it” [Āl ʿImrān 3:97].

With a prohibition, what is sought is non-existence, which is the original state; so what is intended is that the original non-existence should continue, and that is possible and involves nothing beyond one's ability. This too is questionable,
for the urge to commit sins may be strong, such that the servant has no patience to hold back from the sin when he is able to commit it,

and refraining from it then requires a hard struggle, perhaps harder on the soul than merely struggling with oneself to perform an act of obedience. That is why one often finds people who strive and perform acts of obedience but lack the strength to leave forbidden things.
ʿUmar was asked about people who desire sin but do not act on it. He said: “Those are people whose hearts Allah has tested for taqwā; for them is forgiveness and a great reward” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:3].
Yazīd ibn Maysarah said: Allah says in one of the scriptures: O young man who leaves his desire, who spends his youth for My sake, you are with Me like one of My angels.
He said: How intense desire is in the body! It is like a blazing fire; how can those who abstain from women escape it?

The truth of the matter is that Allah does not burden His servants with deeds beyond their capacity, and He has relieved them of many deeds on the mere ground of hardship, as a concession and a mercy to them. As for prohibitions, however, He has not excused anyone for committing them on the ground of strong urges and desires;

rather, He has charged them with leaving them in every situation, and what He has permitted of forbidden foods in necessity is only as much as keeps one alive, not for pleasure and appetite. From this one knows the soundness of Imam Aḥmad's statement: Prohibition is stricter than command.

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, in the hadith of Thawbān and others, that he said: “Be upright, though you will never manage it fully” — that is, you will never be able to achieve uprightness completely.
Al-Ḥakam ibn Ḥazn al-Kulafī narrated: I came in a delegation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and attended the Friday prayer with him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood leaning on a staff or a bow,

praised Allah and extolled Him in a few light, good and blessed words, and then said: “O people, you will not be able — or, you will not do — all that I have commanded you; but aim for what is right and rejoice in good news.” Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded it.

His words ﷺ, “When I command you something, do of it as much as you are able,” are evidence that someone who cannot do all of what he is commanded but can do part of it should do as much of it as he can. This holds consistently across a number of questions.

One is purification. If someone can do part of it but not the rest — whether for lack of water or because of an illness in some of his limbs and not others — he does what he can of it and performs tayammum for the rest. This applies equally to wuḍūʾ and ghusl, according to the well-known position.
Another is prayer. Whoever cannot perform the obligatory prayer standing prays sitting, and if he cannot do that he prays lying down. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.” If he cannot do any of that, he gestures with his eyes and prays with his intention, and the prayer does not lapse for him, according to the well-known position.

Another is zakāt al-fiṭr: if someone can give part of a ṣāʿ, he must do so, according to the correct view. As for someone who can fast part of the day but not complete it, he is not obliged to do so, without disagreement,
because fasting part of a day is not an act of nearness in itself. Likewise, if someone can free only part of a slave in an expiation, he is not obliged to do so,
because freeing a slave in part is not something the Lawgiver loves; on the contrary, one is commanded to complete it by every means.
As for someone who misses the standing at ʿArafah in Ḥajj: does he perform what remains of it — staying the night at Muzdalifah and stoning the pillars — or not,

confining himself instead to circumambulation and running [between Ṣafā and Marwah] and leaving iḥrām by means of an ʿUmrah? There are two reported positions from Aḥmad, the better known being that he confines himself to circumambulation and running,

because staying the night and stoning are appendages of the standing at ʿArafah and follow from it. Allah the Exalted commanded remembering Him at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām [al-Baqarah 2:198], and on the appointed days [al-Baqarah 2:203], only for those who have pressed on from ʿArafāt; so someone who has not stood at ʿArafah is not commanded to do so, just as someone performing ʿUmrah is not.
